titre: Ultramarine, the Blue That Cost More Than Gold
accroche: The blue of a Virgin's cloak came from a stone imported from Afghanistan, purified by hand, and it sometimes cost more than gold.
contenu_vulgarise:
In an old painting, some blues are a matter of geography. Ultramarine, whose name means "beyond the sea," is a pigment made from lapis lazuli, a semi-precious stone that had to be imported into Europe from Badakhshan, in present-day Afghanistan, one of the very few places where it occurs naturally.

## The Price of a Color

You cannot simply crush the stone into powder: the result would be a greyish blue with no intensity. Lapis lazuli contains lazurite, the blue mineral, mixed with other minerals, including calcite and pyrite, fool's gold, which leaves tiny golden flecks in it. More than half the stone is made of these grey, yellow and above all white minerals. To get rid of them, painters followed a long method: they ground the stone, then kneaded it with a paste of resin, beeswax and oil to make a fist-sized ball. A week or two later, they rinsed it under water while kneading: the blue came loose, the impurities stayed behind in the paste. The operation was repeated several times, the first washes giving the purest blue and the later ones increasingly pale, grey blues.

This effort, added to the difficulty of obtaining the stone, explains the price. In the seventeenth century, according to the research team that wrote it in 2020, ultramarine cost more than gold. For the National Gallery in London, this blue was even, at times, more expensive than gold, and it remained a rare and precious color until the nineteenth century.

## What X-Rays Found

In 2020, researchers from the Rijksmuseum, the University of Amsterdam, VU Amsterdam and the European synchrotron in Grenoble published in *Science Advances* a method that makes it possible to trace one detail of this preparation. Some old recipes call for heating the stone red-hot before grinding it. By recreating the extraction in the lab, the team found that without this heating, extraction was significantly more difficult. Through X-ray analysis of small paint samples, they can now tell, more than four hundred years later, whether the lapis lazuli in a painting was heated. The recipes also recommended washing the pigment out with "the hands of a young girl": in the experiment, the men on the team were unable to cleanly isolate the ultramarine, while the female students succeeded.

## A Blue Tied to Rank

The National Gallery notes that the pigment's expense linked it to high status: it was often used to emphasize important features in paintings, such as the clothes worn by the Virgin Mary. The blue of a Virgin's cloak can therefore also be read as a sign of value, and not only as a color.

repere.texte: In the seventeenth century, the pigment ultramarine cost more than gold. A 2020 X-ray study makes it possible to tell whether lapis lazuli was heated red-hot before grinding, a step some old recipes mention, more than four hundred years later.
repere.source: Rijksmuseum, University of Amsterdam, VU Amsterdam, and ESRF, Science Advances, 2020

carte.punch: The blue of the Virgin's cloak sometimes cost more than gold.
carte.idee: Ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli imported from Badakhshan, required long purification. In the seventeenth century it cost more than gold. Its expense tied it to rank: it was often used for the Virgin's clothes.

quiz.question: What made ultramarine so expensive?
choix: A rare Mediterranean shellfish that had to be harvested in huge quantities
A Church tax on any color used to depict the Virgin
A stone imported from Afghanistan, whose blue then had to be laboriously purified
A tropical plant grown only in a few monasteries
quiz.explication: According to the National Gallery, ultramarine was expensive because the mineral was hard to obtain, imported from Badakhshan, and because it needed lengthy processing to purify it. It does not come from a shellfish or a plant, and no Church tax is involved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the name "ultramarine" given to this pigment mean?
choix: The blue of the sea, referring to its color
Beyond the sea, because the stone came from Afghanistan
Sold overseas, referring to its trade in England
Dyed twice, to set it apart from a paler blue
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says the name ultramarine means beyond the sea, because the lapis lazuli was shipped in from Badakhshan, in Afghanistan, one of the only places where this stone exists.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 2020 X-ray analysis make it possible to know about an old painting?
choix: Whether the lapis lazuli stone was heated red-hot before being ground
Who painted it, from the chemical makeup of the blue
The exact age of the painting, to within a few years
The precise country of origin of the stone used
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Rijksmuseum team recreated the extraction in the lab and showed that heating the stone makes purification easier, which makes it possible to tell, more than four hundred years later, whether a painting went through that step.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the 2020 experiment recreating the pigment's purification, who managed to cleanly isolate ultramarine?
choix: The men on the team, by following the recipe exactly
None of the researchers, the operation having failed for everyone
The female students on the team, while the men did not succeed
An algorithm that automated the washing of the pigment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Old recipes recommended washing the pigment with the hands of a young girl; in the experiment, the men on the team were unable to cleanly isolate ultramarine, unlike the female students.
